lines: PRESIDENT:  Thank you.
Before we call the last factual witness for the
respondent, I think it will be very useful if we can
get dates from the both counsel for the quantum expert
from the respondent, for his additional report
regarding the new document filed by the claimant, and
if there is any joint report as well.
Plus, any view for the hearing on July, on the
week commencing 13th July, if there is any
availability, you could share it with the tribunal so
the tribunal can give a direction.  If not end of
today, it should be tomorrow, if we have to sit for
tomorrow as well.
Is that clear?
MR BURKE:  Yes, sir.
Just on availability, and it may help to plan, my
availability for that week is now much better than it
was.  The hearing that I had that week has been stayed
for settlement discussions.  So I'm available any day
that week and that may make it easier to arrange a
date that we both can do.  I know there was otherwise
some difficulty with clashing dates.
MR WYGAS:  So, sir, on that point, then, the Tuesday,
Wednesday or Thursday, the 14th, 15th, 16th, are
available.
PRESIDENT:  15, 14, 16?
MR WYGAS:  Yes.  14, 15, 16.  Yes.
PRESIDENT:  Did both of you check with your experts?
MR BURKE:  Yes.  Yeah.  My expert's available any day
that week.
PRESIDENT:  15, 14, 16.  And your expert, Mr Wygas?
MR WYGAS:  Yeah, my expert Mr Barry could do the 14th,
15th or 16th.
PRESIDENT:  So 14, 15 and 16.
MR WYGAS:  Yeah.
PRESIDENT:  Tribunal member, any view?
DR TALEB:  15 is okay.
PRESIDENT:  Adrian?
MR COLE:  Yeah, those dates are fine with me.
And just to check, those dates are sufficient for
the experts to do their necessary analysis and joint
statement, are they?
MR BURKE:  I think that all rather depends on how long
Mr Barry needs for his work.  I do think it would be
sensible to build in time for a joint statement.
MR COLE:  Yeah.  So do we have Mr Barry's position on
this?
MR WYGAS:  We're waiting for that.  As I understand it,
we're waiting for that.  But we think, once we've got
a date in the diary, if we're going for the 15th, we
can work backwards.
PRESIDENT:  Yeah.
MR WYGAS:  Just looking at the diary now, aim for a joint
statement around --
PRESIDENT:  The 8th?
MR WYGAS:  The 8th is, sir, precisely the date I was
going to go for, and therefore Mr Barry's report on
the 1st.
PRESIDENT:  Yeah, that makes sense.
MR COLE:  And that gives him sufficient time, does it?
Because I'm conscious that in the application there
are various estimates provided, I think up to seven or
eight weeks, in order to analyse the new documents.
MR WYGAS:  There were various estimates provided.
It's like all these things, sir; until you've got
into the detail, you don't know for certain.
MR COLE:  Sure.
MR WYGAS:  Mr Barry estimates were based on doing
things -- looking at documents individually rather
than necessarily together, and he may well be able to
get further resources in relation to that.  So if
there is a problem, then we'll have to come back to
the tribunal.
PRESIDENT:  Yeah.
MR COLE:  Thank you.
PRESIDENT:  I think this is what I was thinking.  So
we'll lock a date for now, 1st July for respondent.
We're going to give a direction by email.  Just
verbally, maybe 1st July for Mr Barry to submit his
additional report, then 8th July for a joint report,
if there is any joint report.  Then 15 for the
continuing with the experts' quantum hearing.
If we need to adjust those dates for any reason,
of course both parties will have liberty to ask the
tribunal for any adjustment or any additional date.
Okay.  If this is okay now, so let's call the last
factual witness for the respondent.
MR BURKE:  While we're doing that, sir, you asked me
yesterday morning for an update on the amount of time
that we had left between us.
PRESIDENT:  Yes.
MR BURKE:  I think we have agreed overnight or first
thing this morning that the claimant has 300-and --
these are very precise figures and may be
unnecessarily precise as things are transpiring.
323 minutes we have left, and the respondent has
483 minutes.
PRESIDENT:  Okay.  That's very useful.  Thank you.
As long as there is agreement between both of you,
so the tribunal is --
MR BURKE:  It's certainly agreed between the solicitors
overnight and this morning, I think.
PRESIDENT:  Yes.  All right.
So let's call the witness, then.
I think he's here.  Yes.  Mr Shajahan; is that
right?
MR BATHUSHA SHAJAHAN
WITNESS:  Yeah.  Bathusha Shajahan.  Yes, sir.  Good
morning to everybody.
PRESIDENT:  Good morning.
You will see on the screen now both oath
statement.  One, if you want to swear by almighty God,
or the second one, if you just want to do affirmation.
Which one do you prefer?
WITNESS:  Almighty God.  I have Quran here.
PRESIDENT:  Where is your Quran?  Where is the holy book
you have?
WITNESS:  Yeah, I have here in front of me.
PRESIDENT:  Can you just pull it up for the tribunal just
to --
WITNESS:  Yes.
PRESIDENT:  Okay.  So in this case, can you go with the
first sentence?
WITNESS:  Yes, I state --
PRESIDENT:  Your name.
WITNESS:  Bathusha Shajahan swear by --
PRESIDENT:  If you can repeat again, "I", then full name,
then --
WITNESS:  I, Bathusha Shajahan, swear by almighty God to
say all the truth and nothing but the truth.
PRESIDENT:  Both counsel, I think that would be
sufficient, we don't need to ask him to do
affirmation.
WITNESS:  Yeah.
I, Bathusha Shajahan, do solemnly --
PRESIDENT:  No, no -- yeah, okay.  Go ahead, go ahead.
WITNESS:  Yeah.
Solemnly, sincerely and truly declare and affirm
to say all the truth and nothing but the truth.
PRESIDENT:  Alright.  Thank you.
Yes, Mr Wygas.
Examination-in-chief by MR WYGAS
MR WYGAS:  Mr Shajahan, thank you for that.
Could we have, please --
PRESIDENT:  I'm sorry to interrupt.  I think I have to
ask him about if there is any correction.
Mr Shajahan, do you confirm there is any
correction are required to the content of your witness
statement?  Have you made any correction or?
WITNESS:  No.  I'm stand in that.  I'm standed.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you.
Sorry, thank you.  Please, Mr Wygas.
MR WYGAS:  Could we go to {C16}, please.
Do you recognise that document?
A. I didn't get you, sir.  Sorry, sorry.
Q. Do you recognise that document?
A. Yes.
Q. What is it?
A. Yeah, it is the witness which was content by myself.
Q. Okay.  Can we then go to page 16 of that document,
please?
Can you see a signature on that page?
A. Yeah, it is mine.
Q. Did you read this document before signing it?
A. Yes, I read it, sir.
Q. Is it true to the best of your knowledge and belief?
A. Yes, I read, I did it myself.
Q. Sorry, is it true to the best of your knowledge and
belief?
A. Yes.
Q. Can we go to {C23}, please.
Do you recognise this document?
A. Yes, I can see.
Q. And what is this document?
A. This is the supplement witness statement.
Q. Whose supplemental witness statement?
A. Yeah.  In front of me.  It shows me that supplement
witness statement only.
Q. Yeah.  And whose supplemental witness statement is it?
A. I didn't get you, sir?
Q. Sorry.  Whose statement is this?
A. This is -- I did myself, sir.  This is -- this is mine
also.
Q. Can we go to page 3, please.
A. Yes.
Q. Can you see a signature on that page?
A. Yeah, it is mine, I did myself.
Q. Did you read this document before signing it?
A. Yes, I did, sir.
Q. And is it true to the best of your knowledge and
belief?
A. Yes.
MR WYGAS:  Thank you very much.
If you just wait there, please, that'd be great.
A. Thank you.
Cross-examination by MR BURKE
MR BURKE:  Mr Shajahan, good morning.
A. Good morning, sir.
Q. You are currently chief accountant for Down Town.  Is
that right?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. You say in your witness statement that I think you
were promoted to chief accountant in 2023; is that
right?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. Can you remember when in 2023?  Which month?
A. It was from January, sir.
Q. January.  So you were chief accountant for the whole
A. Yes.
Q. Okay.  You say in your first witness statement that
part of your role now as chief accountant is to
oversee payroll processing; is that right?
A. Yes.
Q. Did you have a role in payroll processing before your
promotion?  So when you were a senior accountant, you
were involved in payroll processing then?
A. I didn't get you, sir?
Q. When you were senior accountant, so your previous role
from 2019.
A. Okay.
Q. Did you also have any involvement in payroll
processing then?
A. Yes, I did, yes.
Q. If Mr Varghese -- you know who Mr Varghese is, I'm
sure, the contract manager for Down Town?
A. Yes.
Q. If he had wanted information as to the status of
salary payments, if he'd wanted to know whether
salaries had been paid or not, would he have asked
you?
A. No, he didn't ask about it.  He does not --
Q. He didn't ask you?
A. Yeah, it is not -- that is not his part of it, to ask.
Q. So Mr Varghese never asked you personally about
whether salaries had been paid; is that right?
A. No, sir, he didn't ask.
Q. Do you know whether he asked anybody in the Down Town
finance team whether salaries have been paid?  I'm
talking about 2023, specifically.
A. No, sir.  They didn't ask about it, sir.
Q. So Mr Varghese never asked anyone in the finance team
whether salaries had been paid?
A. No, sir.
Q. Okay.
You say in your witness statement, you talk about
salary payments in several parts of your witness
statement, and I think you very fairly accept that
there were delays to the payment of worker and staff
salaries, yes?
A. During this project started, sir, we, the Down Town
had a consistent salary disbursement record.  While
the project progressed, the unplanned cost and --
Q. Mr Shajahan, apologies for interrupting.
I would quite like to get finished with you quite
quickly this morning, so that we have the time and
hopefully finish the hearing today.
If you could listen very carefully to my question
and just answer the question, then we'll be more --
we'll do it more quickly.
The question I asked was whether you accepted --
I'm not asking the reasons why at the moment -- but
whether you accepted that there had been delays by
Down Town to the payment of salaries to workers and
staff?
A. During the contract period, we don't have any delay.
After the addendum 4, we had some issues because of
some payments delayed from our claimant.
Q. So your evidence is that before addendum number 4, so
before February 2023 --
A. Yes.
Q. -- there were no delays to the payment of salaries.
Is that your evidence?
A. Yes, sir.  We don't have any delay.  But during the
Covid time we had some delays, but it was paid on
time.
Q. Okay.  Well, let's look at that, Mr Shajahan.
Paragraph -- maybe before that: you would accept that
delaying the payment of workers and staff should be an
absolute last resort.  You should do everything you
can to make sure you pay people on time.  Yes?
A. Yes, sir.  We paid on time, yeah.
Q. Yes.  And it's important that if Down Town possibly
can, it pays people on time?
A. Yes, yes.
Q. If we look please at paragraph 6.3 of your first
witness statement.
A. Yes.
Q. And you're talking here about the period prior to
addendum number 4, so prior to February 2023.
A. Yes.
Q. You say:
"... while already under financial pressure,
DownTown maintained a semblance of stability.  We had
not yet fully depleted the working capital reserves we
had built from previous successful projects.  Our
balance sheet showed healthy, though declining,
retained earnings.  We could still access credit lines
and manage our obligations, albeit with increasing
difficulty."
Do you see that?
A. Yes, yes.  During the time before the addendum 4 and
between December to February, there was a incentive
plan period.  A milestone was there.  And at that time
we were done our job, but we didn't --
Q. Mr Shajahan, apologies again.  I just asked you if you
saw the paragraph of the witness statement I was
talking about.  I didn't ask you any other question.
Based on what you say in this paragraph, paragraph
6.3, it is right that as at February 2023, Down Town
still had working capital reserves, yes?
A. Yes, we had from our other projects.
Q. And it is right that as at February 2023, Down Town
had access to credit lines, correct?
A. Yes.
Q. And it's right to say that as at February 2023,
Down Town had a healthy balance sheet, correct?
A. Yes, sir.  That is from other projects.
Q. Yes.  So there is no reason -- you've agreed with me
already that delaying payments to staff and workers is
a last resort.  There's no reason why before
February 2023, Down Town should have been late in
paying any of its people; correct?
A. Yes, yes.
Q. Can we go, please, to {E41}.  This is a letter dated
19th November 2019.  Have you -- I suspect you
haven't.  Have you seen this letter before?  It's just
on your screen.
Have you seen this letter before, Mr Shajahan?
A. Yes.
Q. You have.  When did you see it last?  Can you
remember?  Can you remember when you last saw this
letter?  Is it recently?
A. Yes.
Q. Can you remember when you last saw this letter,
Mr Shajahan?  (Pause)
Can you hear me, Mr Shajahan?
A. Yeah, yeah, I can read it, yeah.
Q. When did you last see this letter?
A. This is on 23rd November 2019.
Q. Yes, but when -- I asked you if you'd seen it before
and you said you had.  When did you last see it?  Have
you seen it recently?  Is it in the last few weeks
that you've seen this letter?
A. No, no, no, sir.  I was seeing very long before.
I was not remember this.
Q. Okay.  That may be the reason.
We see in the first bullet point -- so this is a
letter from TTSJV to Down Town.  It's addressed to
Mr Shaikh Al Khalifa.
Who is he?  "To the attention", at the top of the
page?  It says:
"Att[ention]: Mr. Shaikh Isa Bin Ali Abdulla
Al Khalifa".
Who is he?
A. Yeah, he's the director of the company.
Q. Is he the managing director of the company?
A. Yes.
Q. Is he the owner?  Does he own the company?
A. Yeah, he's the managing director of the company.
Q. Is he also the owner, or is he also an owner?
A. I didn't get you?
Q. Is he also a part owner of Down Town?  Does he own any
part of Down Town?
A. Yes, he's owner of the company, yes.
Q. He's the owner of the company?
A. Yes.
Q. You see the letter is addressed to him and we see that
TTSJV is telling Mr Al Khalifa that there's been an HR
audit on 12th November, 2019.  That's the first line,
do you see that?  First line of the letter:
"During the daily walkthrough and subsequent HR
Audit carried out on 12th Nov 2019 ..."
Do you see that?
A. No, it was came as a information only.  I was seen,
I was seeing it in the beginning, at very beginning.
But I'm not much aware of it.  This was deal by our HR
department.  So I was not the decision making here in
that to be part of it.
Q. That wasn't the question I asked you, Mr Shajahan.
We can see from this that TTSJV has carried out an
HR audit on 12th November 2019.  And one of the things
that audit has revealed, and this is the first bullet
point in the bullet-pointed list, is that there has
been a two-month delay in salary payment to people
from Down Town working on this project; correct?
A. Yeah, it was mentioned here like.
Q. Yes.  So this is November 2019 and the last salary
they had been paid was in August 2019.  Do you see
that?
A. Yeah, it is mentioned here.  I can see here.
Q. This is only about six weeks into the subcontract
period, yes?  Subcontract was signed on
1st September 2019, yes?
A. Yes, at the beginning.
Q. So these payment delays, they cannot be said to be the
result of TTSJV not paying anything, can they?
They're not TTSJV's fault that Down Town hadn't paid
these salaries, is it?
A. No, it is -- it is in the stage of startup.
I'm not -- unsure about much about it, this point
here.
Q. Do you remember there being delays to the payment of
salaries in 2019?  You would have been a senior
accountant in the business at that point.
A. Yes, I was there.  I was seen the payments was paid on
time.  We don't have any delayed.  The date was
mentioned already in that, what -- which month we are
paid.  Everything was submitted in that time.  We
don't have any delay at that time.
Q. So your evidence is, your recollection is that this
letter is just wrong.  There hadn't been any payment
delays.  Is that right?
A. No, we didn't receive this one.  We just seen it only.
But the salary was paid at that time.
Q. I'm asking you, Mr Shajahan, for your recollection,
your evidence.  Is your evidence that this letter is
just wrong; as at November 2019, there had not been
any delays to the payment of Down Town salaries.  Is
that your evidence?
A. No.  This letter I seen after long time.  In the
middle.  Even this was not seen in that -- on that
time, particular time.  It was seen in the middle
only, maybe in the middle of 2020 I have seen this
letter, but I was not seen in the beginning, at the
time of this number.
Q. Well, I'm asking you about the letter now,
Mr Shajahan.  You were senior accountant when this
letter was received.  You were involved in payroll
processing.  You've agreed with me on both of those
points; yes?
A. Yes, but we paid --
Q. And can you remember in your role as senior accountant
with involvement in payroll processing, do you recall
there being delays to the payment of worker salaries
in August, September, October and November of 2019?
A. As of my remember, we do not have any delays in that
time.
Q. So Down Town's response to this would have been: we
don't know what you're talking about, we've paid all
the salaries.
Is that right?
A. Yes.  I'm talking about salaries.  We had paid on time
at that time.
Q. Okay.  What day of the month do Down Town's employment
contracts say that people should be paid?
A. As per Bahrain law, we paid the salaries on time.  On
time, we paid.
Q. The employment contracts, Down Town employment
contracts say that people are entitled to be paid on
or before the 10th of the following month.  Yes?
A. Yes, yes.
Q. If we go, please, to {E43}.
This is Down Town's reply, signed by Mr Varghese,
dated 21st November.  So it's a few days afterwards.
Do you remember having seen this letter
previously, Mr Shajahan?
Do you recall this letter, Mr Shajahan?  It's no
criticism if you don't.
A. Yes, sir.  It was -- I was not seen this letter, but.
Q. What Mr Varghese is saying in this letter, this is the
first bullet point, and this letter is dated 21st
November 2019.  In response to the complaint that
salaries are late, it says:
"It was stated in your letter that we have paid
salaries up to August 2019.  This is not correct, we
paid salaries for all our employees up to September...
and certain sites up to October 2019."
So Mr Varghese is accepting this letter that
salaries, some salaries, were late, wasn't it?
A. Yeah.  He's mentioned that he paid it, we paid it on
September and October, some certain --
Q. No, he's not, Mr Shajahan.  He's saying that only some
of the October salaries, by late November, only some
of the October salaries had been paid.  Isn't that
what he's saying?
A. Yeah, and certain --
Q. That's why he says:
"... and certain sites up to October 2019."
A. Up to October, yes, it is mentioned.  Yeah, it is
mentioned.
Q. So he's saying, he doesn't agree with the extent of
the issue, but he is admitting, he is accepting that
there are some salaries that are late, isn't he?
A. Yes.
Q. And there is no excuse, you've already accepted, for
paying salaries late prior to February 2023, was
there?
A. At 2023 we severely stuck in the funds during the
time.
Q. Yes.  Mr Shajahan, this letter is November 2019.  This
is when you had a healthy balance sheet and access to
lines of credit, wasn't it?
A. Yeah.  The healthy balance sheet were from the other
project only, not --
Q. I accept that, Mr Shajahan -- or at least I accept
that's your evidence.
But you've agreed that paying people late is
a last resort.  And if you have the reserves, if you
had the availability of funds to pay, you should have
been paying people on time, shouldn't you?  (Pause)
Shouldn't you, Mr Shajahan?
A. Yes, sir, but, yeah, we pay --
Q. Why, if you can recall -- and it's fine if you don't.
But why were these salaries being paid late in 2019?
A. At that period, some prioritise expenditure.  If you
are not paid, that will be the stop of job also, that
we couldn't able to stop at that time.  So we are in
the initial stage of set-up time, though at that time
we were focusing at that time for the sites
mobilisations.
Q. I'm sorry, I'm not sure I understand that answer,
Mr Shajahan.  If you had --
A. We are in the initial stage.
Q. -- availability of funds and access to credit to pay
salaries, why were you prioritising paying for other
things, rather than paying people what they were owed?
A. We -- on time we submitted salaries, sir, but there
was delays.  It was everything was paid on time.
Q. Well, that's not what this letter says, is it,
Mr Shajahan?  (Pause)
Should we look at another letter?  {E589}.
This is a letter two years later, October 2021.
We see another complaint.  This is well before
February 2023, correct?
A. Yes.
Q. This is a period when Down Town still had working
capital reserves, a healthy balance sheet and access
to lines of credit; correct?
A. Sir, we had a healthy balance sheet, but it was not on
time we received funds.
Q. But Mr Shajahan, if you had a healthy balance sheet,
working capital reserves and access to lines of
credit?
A. Even we --
Q. You should have been paying your people on time,
shouldn't you?
A. Even we have a healthy balance sheet, we are not
having inflow at that time to pay these people.  Maybe
we have it by receivables, but we are not having by on
time cash inflows, so we couldn't able to pay it at
that time.
Q. So is your evidence that even well before
February 2023, the financial situation of Down Town
was such that it could not afford to pay people on
time?  Is that your evidence?
A. That is the reason I'm telling.  During the Covid
pandemic time, we face a lot of challenges during the
time and the workforce we couldn't able to make, and
we are only getting our payments by the productions
only.  That productions also very less.  There was a
lockdown happen and people are -- we are keeping in
the quarantine and we feed them three time food and
this all unpredicted, unbudgeted expenses was happened
at that time.
So this all led to our delay comes in the
salaries.  Sometimes.
Q. Mr Shajahan, I'm really struggling to understand your
evidence, because you've said in your witness
statement and you've confirmed today that before
February 2023, Down Town had healthy balance sheets,
working capital reserves, access to lines of credit.
So I'm struggling to understand why, if that's
right, why, well before 2023, you would have not been
paying your people on time.
Can you help me with that, Mr Shajahan?  Could you
explain why Down Town would not have been using its
access to credit and its reserves to pay its people?
A. That's what I'm saying.  We had a healthy balance
sheet, but we are not having as a inflow at the right
time, so that to pay the salaries.  We had a
receivables as a healthy way, but we are not having on
time salaries because everybody got stuck.  The whole
pandemic period, everybody got stuck.  We are facing
problems.  Everybody got facing problems for getting
monies, getting funds.
So everybody got stuck at that time.  So we
couldn't able to pay at that time on time.
Q. Is your evidence, Mr Shajahan, that even though
Down Town had access -- had funds or had access to
funds to pay its people on time, it chose not to?  Is
that your evidence?
A. No, we don't had a fund.  If we had a fund, we will be
prioritise that to be paid salaries.
Q. So you didn't, in fact, have the funds in 2019, 2020,
2021 and 2022 to pay people on time?  Is that your
evidence?
A. No, not like that.  It was some delay happened during
the time of Covid pandemic time, but we were paid it.
There was some few days' delay, but if come -- the
bigger delay, if comes, the Bahrain law will not allow
to work.  People, they will complain, but that not
happens.  We were paid on time peoples.  Maybe a few
days' delay it happened, but we paid it.
Q. Mr Shajahan, is your evidence that there were no
complaints from people who weren't paid on time before
February 2023?
A. Yes, for the salaries, we don't have any complaint.
We don't have any complaint in the -- anywhere.  Even
the LMRA were --
Q. Are you sure about that, Mr Shajahan?
A. Yes.
Q. You don't remember large numbers of Down Town
workforce going on strike in 2022 because they hadn't
been paid?
A. No, we don't had any strikes during that time.
Q. You didn't have any strikes in 2022?  That's your
evidence?
A. Yes, sir.  We don't had any strikes.  There are some
other companies we heard that strikes happen, but we
don't had any strikes.
Q. Are you sure about that, Mr Shajahan?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. Okay.  Just bear with me one second, Mr Shajahan.
(Pause)
Just one second.
Can we please go to {E1150}.
See the date of this letter?  24th September 2022.
Did you see the letter, Mr Shajahan?
A. Yeah, I can see here:
"NOTICE OF DEFAULT -- WORK STOPPAGE DUE TO
SUBCONTRACTOR'S EMPLOYEES STRIKE ..."
The subcontractor, do notice.  Subcontractor, not
our employees.
Q. Are you suggesting this isn't a letter to Down Town,
Mr Shajahan?  Do you think the reference to
"subcontractor" is somebody else in this letter?  Is
that your evidence?
A. No, it is not our employees.
Q. Do you see who this is addressed to?  It's addressed
to Down Town Construction; yes?
A. Yeah.
Q. And it's addressed to Mr Varghese.  And you see what
the subject matter of the letter is: employee strikes
in brownfield units on the Bapco project.  Do you see
that?
A. Yeah, I can see this, but I don't --
Q. And you see the first sentence of the first paragraph:
"CONTRACTOR has been made aware of a massive
strike action of SUBCONTRACTOR'S employees which
started on Thursday, 22 September 2022, involved
around 800 people and still is ongoing up to now.  The
strike is primarily aimed at protesting against
continuous payment delay of salary according to the
applicable Law (before every 10th of the month)."
And then there are some contractual references
about the breaches of contract that constitutes.  Do
you see that, Mr Shajahan?
A. We never seen -- like, the people, like the
